readerTitle: When your customers get a raise, some of your products lose
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가족의 장바구니, 할인 슈퍼마켓, 대기업 안의 소프트웨어 제품팀) + 실제 연구 (엥겔의 법칙)
insight: 고객의 소득이 바뀌면 수요는 한 방향으로 움직이지 않는다. 각 제품이 고객에게 '올라가는 단계'인지 '형편이 어려울 때의 선택'인지에 따라 방향이 갈린다.
misconception: 고객의 소득이 오르면 모든 제품이 더 팔리고, 소득이 줄면 모든 제품이 덜 팔린다.

sources.text: Engel, E. (1857). Die Productions- und Consumtionsverhältnisse des Königreichs Sachsen (엥겔의 법칙)
장바구니, 슈퍼마켓, 소프트웨어 제품팀 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 엥겔의 1857년 연구: 벨기에 노동자 가구 예산 자료(Ducpétiaux 수집)를 분석해 소득이 오를수록 식비 비중이 줄어든다는 결론을 냈다는 내용을 확인하세요. 카드에는 '1857년, 가계 예산 연구'로만 적었습니다.
소득탄력성 정의: 수요량 변화율 ÷ 소득 변화율. 양수면 정상재, 음수면 열등재. 카드의 예시(소득 10% 상승, 판매 5% 하락 → −0.5)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산 확인: −5 ÷ 10 = −0.5.
가상 소프트웨어 요금제 $20, $80은 설명용입니다. 실제 기업 수치가 아닙니다.

cards.title: When your customers get a raise, some of your products lose
body: A family gets a 15% raise. Their grocery bill goes up. But look closer at the cart.
The instant noodles are gone. So is the giant bag of the cheapest rice. In their place: fresh pasta, a branded coffee, a ready-made salad. More money came in, and some products lost a customer.

image.label: Two shopping carts from the same family, before and after a raise
image.brief: 같은 가족의 장바구니 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽 'Before'에는 인스턴트 라면, 큰 포대 쌀, 무명 브랜드 빵. 오른쪽 'After'에는 생파스타, 원두커피, 샐러드. 왼쪽에서 사라진 물건 위에 점선 윤곽만 남김. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: A big employer in town just raised wages.
body: You run a discount grocery store. The town's largest factory raised pay, and local household incomes are up about 15%.
What should you expect for your cheapest store-brand basics?

options.text: Sales of everything rise, so order more of every item
options.feedback: Total spending likely rises, but not evenly. You could end up with shelves of budget basics that shoppers are now trading away from.

options.text: Basics may fall while branded and fresh items grow, so shift the mix
options.feedback: This follows where the extra money actually goes. The cost is some guesswork on which items flip, so watch the first few weeks of sales closely.

options.text: Nothing changes, because people need food either way
options.feedback: True that food demand doesn't vanish. But people still eat, they just eat differently, and the mix inside the cart is what moves.

cards.title: The cart grows, but not evenly.
body: Over the next months, total sales climb. Fresh produce, branded snacks and ready meals grow fastest.

But the cheapest bread, the bulk rice and the store-brand noodles slip. Shoppers didn't stop eating those foods because they disliked them. They bought them because money was tight. When it got less tight, they moved on.

image.label: Product shelf with green up arrows and red down arrows
image.brief: 슈퍼마켓 선반 일러스트. 생과일, 샐러드, 원두커피 위에 초록색 위쪽 화살표, 라면, 대용량 쌀, 무명 브랜드 빵 위에 빨간색 아래쪽 화살표. 상단에 'Incomes +15%' 배너. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Normal goods and inferior goods
body: When incomes rise, people buy more of **normal goods** and less of **inferior goods**. "Inferior" says nothing about quality. It means the thing people buy when money is short.

Economists measure this with *income elasticity of demand*: the percent change in sales divided by the percent change in income. If incomes rise 10% and noodle sales fall 5%, that's −0.5. A minus sign means inferior. A plus sign means normal.

image.label: A scale from negative to positive income elasticity
image.brief: 가로 눈금자 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 음수 영역 'Inferior: buy less as income rises'(라면, 대용량 쌀 아이콘), 가운데 0, 오른쪽 양수 영역 'Normal: buy more as income rises'(외식, 여행 아이콘). 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: An old pattern in household budgets
body: In 1857, the statistician Ernst Engel studied the budgets of working families. He found that as income rises, households spend more on food in total, but food takes a **smaller share** of the budget.
This pattern, now called Engel's law, has held up in many countries since. The extra money doesn't vanish. It moves toward other things, and inside food it moves toward different foods.

cards.title: The same product can go both ways.
body: Whether a product is normal or inferior depends on who buys it. A store-brand coffee is an upgrade for a student who drank instant. It's a downgrade for a manager who used to buy from a café.

It also runs in reverse. When incomes fall, inferior goods can gain. Discount stores, repair shops and budget plans often get busier when customers feel squeezed. So the useful question is: **what do my customers trade up to, and what do they trade down from?**

cards.title: Incomes rarely change alone.
body: A wage rise often arrives with higher prices, new rivals or changing tastes. If sales of a basic item fall, income may not be the reason.

The signs also lag. Many people change habits only after a raise feels permanent. Read income effects as one force among several, and test them against your own sales data before reshaping a whole range.

cards.title: Now you lead a product team inside a big software company.
body: Your team sells booking software to small restaurants: Basic at $20 a month, Pro at $80. Restaurant revenues in your market are falling.
Leadership asks what to plan for. What do you tell them?

options.text: Expect fewer sign-ups on both plans and cut Basic marketing
options.feedback: It saves budget now, but Basic may be the plan squeezed customers move to. Cutting it pushes them toward cancelling instead of downgrading.

options.text: Expect Pro downgrades, Basic to hold or grow, and make downgrading easy
options.feedback: You may lose revenue per customer but keep the customer. That trade looks better when restaurant incomes recover and some move back to Pro.

options.text: Expect no change, because restaurants rely on the software
options.feedback: Reliance keeps many customers, but it doesn't keep them on the same plan. Planning for no change leaves you surprised by downgrades.

cards.title: When incomes move, ask which way each product moves.
body: Some products gain when customers have more money. Others gain when customers have less. Knowing which is which tells you what to stock, promote and protect.
**Try it today:** list your three main products. For each, write what a customer would switch to with 20% more money, and with 20% less.
